Thick
thik
a. (dense; of great depth between surfaces; rendering Hebrew arafel in thick darkness, ab in thick clouds)
From the Saxon thicce, dense. In the KJV the adjective is most often attached to darkness, clouds, boughs, and bosses — things whose density either hides or protects, which is why it becomes a word about God's nearness rather than his distance.

Biblical Definition

Thick in the Authorized Version is chiefly the density that hides. Its great verse is Sinai's: “And the people stood afar off, and Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was” (Exodus 20:21). The two halves are one of the sharpest contrasts in Scripture — the people stand back from the darkness, Moses walks into it, and the reason is given in four words, where God was. The thick darkness is not the absence of God but the covering of his presence; it hides him because he cannot be looked upon, and the mediator goes in. David uses the same picture in his song of deliverance: God “made darkness pavilions round about him, dark waters, and thick clouds of the skies” (2 Samuel 22:12) — the imagery of the storm theophany, where the density is the tent he dwells in. The word also serves the ordinary and the ominous. Job describes a man charging God like a soldier “upon the thick bosses of his bucklers” (Job 15:26), running at the Almighty behind the thickest part of a shield. And Ezekiel measures the pride of Assyria by height: a cedar in Lebanon of high stature, “and his top was among the thick boughs” (Ezekiel 31:3) — a tree so tall it stood in the canopy, and the chapter is about its felling.

Webster 1828 Definition

Dense. Its chief use is the thick darkness of Sinai, which the people stood back from and Moses entered where God was — density that covers the presence rather than marking its absence.

expand to see more

THICK, a. [Sax. thicce.] Dense; not thin; as a thick fluid; a thick vapor.

2. Having more depth or extent from one surface to its opposite than a certain other thing.

3. Close; crowded; set with things near to each other; as a thick forest.

4. Frequent; following each other in quick succession; as, the blows fell thick.

5. THICK, n. The thickest part, or the time when any thing is thickest; as in the thick of the fight.

Key Scripture

Exodus 20:21 — "And the people stood afar off, and Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was."

2 Samuel 22:12 — "And he made darkness pavilions round about him, dark waters, and thick clouds of the skies."

Job 15:26 — "He runneth upon him, even on his neck, upon the thick bosses of his bucklers:"

Ezekiel 31:3 — "Behold, the Assyrian was a cedar in Lebanon with fair branches, and with a shadowing shroud, and of an high stature; and his top was among the thick boughs."

Modern Corruption

God's hiddenness is read as absence or as coldness, when Scripture makes the thick darkness the covering of a presence too great to be looked upon — and gives a mediator to enter it.

expand to see more

When God seems dark, the modern instinct is to conclude either that he is not there or that he is indifferent. Exodus 20:21 answers both in a single clause. The darkness was thick, the people were afraid and stood afar off — and God was in it. Divine hiddenness in Scripture is a function of glory, not of absence: he dwells in the light which no man can approach unto (1 Timothy 6:16), and the same inaccessibility can be described as blazing light or as thick cloud, because the effect on a creature's eyes is the same. This is why the classical attributes matter pastorally. A God who is simple, immutable, and infinite cannot be surveyed by us, and the dark is the shape our not-surveying takes.

The principle to recover is the mediator in the sentence. The people stood afar off; Moses drew near. Israel could not enter the darkness and was not asked to; a man went in on their behalf and came back with the words of God. Hebrews contrasts that mountain of blackness and darkness and tempest with the mount Zion believers have come to, and names the reason for the difference: Jesus the mediator of the new covenant (Hebrews 12:18-24). What Moses did once and partially, Christ has done for ever, and those who are in him are brought inside the cloud rather than kept at the foot of the mountain.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew arafel is heavy gloom or thick darkness, the cloud of Sinai; ab is a thick cloud; abah is to be thick or dense, used of the boughs of a great tree.

expand to see more

Hebrew arafel (H6205) — thick darkness, gloom; the cloud Moses entered at Sinai.

Hebrew ab (H5645) — a thick cloud, a dark mass; the pavilions of 2 Samuel 22:12.

Hebrew abah (H5666) — to be thick, dense; used of a body grown gross and of heavy boughs.

Hebrew choshek (H2822) — darkness; the general term, distinguished from the thick arafel.

Greek gnophos (G1105) — blackness, thick gloom; the word for Sinai's darkness in Hebrews 12:18.

Usage

"Of the darkness Moses entered: Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was (Exodus 20:21)."

"Of the storm as God's pavilion: dark waters, and thick clouds of the skies (2 Samuel 22:12)."

"Of pride grown to the canopy: his top was among the thick boughs (Ezekiel 31:3)."
